description: Turkish core building blocks and conversation words for A2–B1 learners, Standard Turkish (Istanbul norm).

terms.definition: Says something exists, or that someone has it; Turkish uses it instead of a 'have' verb.
terms.example: Köşede bir eczane var. — There's a pharmacy on the corner.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Bir arabaya sahibim' for 'I have a car': say 'Arabam var'.

terms.definition: Turns a statement into a yes/no question. Its vowel matches the last vowel of the word before it.
terms.example: Otobüs Kadıköy'e gider mi? — Does the bus go to Kadıköy?
terms.discussion: Write it as a separate word. With 'you', the person ending moves onto it: Geliyor musun?

terms.definition: Put a verb's dictionary form before istemek to say you want to do it.
terms.example: Akşam sinemaya gitmek istiyorum. — I want to go to the cinema tonight.
terms.anti_example: Not 'İstiyorum gitmek': the verb you want comes first and istemek goes last. Say 'Gitmek istiyorum'.

terms.definition: Means 'I mean' or 'so': you use it to explain again or to sum up.
terms.example: Çok yorgunum, yani gelmiyorum. — I'm really tired, so I'm not coming.
terms.discussion: Also a filler while you think, like English 'well'. Used a lot, it sounds very casual.

terms.definition: Negates a noun or adjective: 'is not', 'am not'. Verbs take -me / -ma instead.
terms.example: Bu çorba sıcak değil. — This soup isn't hot.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Çorba sıcak yok' for 'The soup isn't hot': yok means 'there is none'. Say 'Çorba sıcak değil'.

terms.definition: Compares: 'like' or 'as', placed after the noun you compare to.
terms.example: Kardeşim bir kedi gibi uyuyor. — My brother sleeps like a cat.
terms.discussion: After ben and sen, say benim gibi and senin gibi, not ben gibi.

terms.definition: Attaches 'can' to a verb stem: gel- becomes gelebil-, then the normal ending follows.
terms.example: Pencereyi açabilir misin? — Can you open the window?
terms.anti_example: Not 'gelebilmiyorum' for 'I can't come': the negative drops -bil-. Say 'gelemiyorum'.

terms.definition: Says something isn't there, or that you don't have it: the other half of var.
terms.example: Maalesef bugün simit yok. — Sorry, no simit today.
terms.discussion: Answer a 'var mı?' question with a bare 'yok'. It sounds more natural than 'hayır'.

terms.definition: Gives your opinion: 'I think', 'in my view'. It usually opens the sentence.
terms.example: Bence bu elbise çok güzel. — I think this dress is really nice.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Düşünüyorum ki elbise güzel' for 'I think the dress is nice': say 'Bence elbise güzel'.

terms.definition: Means 'needed'. Give the verb a 'my' or 'your' ending first to say you have to: gitmem lazım.
terms.example: Artık gitmem lazım. — I have to go now.
terms.discussion: For a thing you need, just add lazım: Bana su lazım (I need water). Very common in speech.

relationships.description: Both translate as 'not' in English, but değil negates a description and yok says something isn't there.
